utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. It's Matthew Olmsted, Tolimir Hans, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for the Stanisic Defence this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours, for Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I correctly advised that there is a preliminary matter with which we must deal before the witness comes in?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is a protective measures issue if we could go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will move into is it closed session or private session, I keep getting it --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the Prosecution begins, may we have your name for the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muharem Krzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had several professions. The last job I did was that of a diplomat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your date of birth is when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 19th of December, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, having given testimony before previously in this Tribunal, you would be aware of the procedure whereby the side calling you, in this case the Prosecution, would have questions of you, and then counsel for each of the accused would have a right to cross-examine you, and after any questions arising out of that, that the Prosecution may have, the Chamber may have questions of you. So I would now invite Mr. Olmsted to begin his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, have you testified previously before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In which case in particular did you testify before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: In the Talic case and the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to listen to your testimony in the Brdjanin and Talic case?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was this audio recording that you listened to an accurate reflection of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that it was very accurate. I didn't have the opportunity to compare documents because some statements were based on documents, but I think it was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, sir, if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked in the Brdjanin case, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Basically, yes. I may -- I may add some details if I were asked these questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would move to admit this witness's 92 ter package, the testimony is 65 ter Exhibits 9070 through 9074, and there's also 16 associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect, the Defence objects. I'm not trying to split the hairs in two, but the rule is very explicit when and how the 92 ter evidence can be offered as exhibits, and I don't think that the witness gave the answers which allowed the -- my learned friend from the opposing side to offer this as evidence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I would be grateful if you could -- and perhaps you may be reluctant to answer my question because then you would be doing the Prosecution's job, but on the face of it I'm not sure that I fully appreciate the basis of your objection to the application for the admission of this witness who is called in the provisions of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, it must be my mistake. Namely, the 92 ter rule provides a certain -- provides certain conditions that have to be met in order that the witness statement and accompanying exhibits can be offered as evidence under the Rule 92 ter. One of these conditions is that the witness confirms that he will give the very same answers on the very same question today as he did in his previous testimonies. Now, hearing the witness here, I don't think he confirmed that in the full length of -- or the full understanding of 92 ter because he said, I would confirm but I would add some other -- at least that was my understanding, that he would like to add some other information or sort of expand on his answers. Therefore, therefore, I don't think that -- that is why I say it is not my wish to split the hair in two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to say, you did preface your remarks by splitting hairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm concerned that if the witness wanted to give more answers than he previously gave in the previous trial, then I don't think that this package is legible for 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, if memory serves, we walked this road before about November or thereabouts, and isn't the practical reality that although a witness is importing what he would have said on a previous occasion, it is unlikely that because no two trials are identical, that the details given in March of 2003 would necessarily be the same as given in January of 2010? Hadn't we had lengthy discussions on this previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, but I think -- I think this discussion that we had was aimed at the different points which we were discussing at the moment. I'm now strictly talking about the application of Rule 92 ter. It says which are the conditions, and I don't think -- I don't think that the condition has been met with the answer that the witness has given. Therefore, either my learned friend can, I don't know, explore that with the witness and then offer it on the 92 ter, because I think at this point he was premature and that's why I objected, with all due respect. I'm sorry to use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's hear from Mr. Olmsted on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The Prosecution respectfully disagrees with the Defence on this issue. The witness said that he listened to his recording, it was very accurate, not just accurate, very accurate. And then he says that, yes, he would answer the questions the same but he'd probably provide additional details. Not different details, additional details. The issue here is, of course, truthfulness, to answer the question truthfully, whether he could provide even more information than he provided on the witness stand, I think probably every witness would probably say that they could have provided more details, sometimes they are not asked for more details, so. But I could certainly ask this witness whether he answered his questions truthfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I note that the witness's answer as it was recorded in the transcript was that the witness offered to add some details to his previous testimony, and maybe what you should do now is then to explore what these details are because otherwise we will be unable to ascertain whether they amount to more than just details. Hold on a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, what we will do in order to save time is simply just to start out with the remarks that you have. We are very aware of the objection made by Mr. Zecevic, and we understand Mr. Zecevic's objection to be that the witness raised the possibility that his testimony today might actually differ substantially from what he said in his previous testimony. However, the Chamber notes that what the witness actually said was just that he might add some details and nothing more than that, and we interpret this to be nothing more than exactly what the witness said, namely that he will stick to his testimony in Brdjanin, but maybe a few details may be added that he, you know, failed to present during his testimony in Brdjanin, but certainly those details would not make his testimony today any different in substance from what it was in Brdjanin. Now, of course, there's always a margin of appreciation here and so rather than trying to find out what these details may be, I think we should just get on with it and then if you find at any point in time that what the witness is now testifying differs substantially from what was in his testimony in Brdjanin, I think then you should raise it, and that's the way we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, does this mean we are not going to be admitting his 92 ter statement at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, we will be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit numbers to be signed are P459.1 through P459.21.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I have one more additional question with regard to your background. From 1991 through 1994, did you hold a political position in Banja Luka municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Legally and formally, yes, but not in the municipality. But on the political level when you say municipality, that could be understood as if I had been a municipal representative. No, I was just the political leader of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. What position -- what political leadership position did you hold during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: First I was the secretary of the democratic action party in Banja Luka when it was founded first. Then I became a member of the Executive Board. And later at one point I was elected vice-president of the party, but that was an ad hoc election within the Main Board when the president left us and that president had been elected by acclamation at one meeting, and then in September/October 1991 I was elected officially at the Assembly meeting which included all the representatives of the SDA, I was elected president.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How long were you president of the SDA for?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: For practical purposes, I was president as long as I lived in Banja Luka, and formerly I remained president until I turned over that duty in 1994 to another member of the Executive Board when we had a meeting in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm now going to show you a map of Banja Luka town and ask you to identify a number of locations on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's 65 ter Exhibit 10213. And the witness will need a digital pen for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may interrupt. Sir, if I understand you well, there is a difference between what you call the practical purposes of your Presidency until as long as you lived in Banja Luka and your formal being a president in 1994. Is there a difference in time? When did you leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left Banja Luka in end October 1993. I left for Zagreb. In my absence, it was not possible to perform that role any more, and I didn't wish to. However, formally and legally, I could be replaced only at an official Assembly meeting of representatives of the SDA. Banja Luka was then under military occupation and it was not possible to organise such a meeting at that time so I used the first opportunity to turn over my responsibilities to another man to give him legitimacy. There was a meeting of representatives who came from free territories and some other representatives who lived abroad and at meeting I turned over my duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we see the exhibit on the screen, please. Perhaps if we could zoom out just first of all. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, is this an accurate map of the centre of Banja Luka town as it existed in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I think so because I've seen the map before and especially when I see the images on the side in the legend. Of course like any map of a large city it can be confusing at first, and I don't know how long it's been since I've seen its image in this form, but I do recognise certain localities that make things clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, along the margins of this map are photographs numbered 1 through 5. Please take a look at the first photograph labelled number 1 and tell us what that building was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is, I think, the former, or perhaps even the current staff of the Krajina Corps. Before that it was the staff of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you mark on the map with a number 1 where that building is approximately located.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: [In English] Just a moment. Somewhere here. Somewhere. I can't -- [Interpretation] I can't recognise the building itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Fair enough. And this is not the most beautiful map, so just do your best that you can to give the Trial Chamber an idea of generally where they are located. If you could look at the second photograph, could you tell us what that building was back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Building number 2 is partially hidden by the trees, and it looks to me like the annex building to the first one, the staff, but it's a separate building where meetings were held, and it housed all sorts of social events, celebrations, and inside there was a restaurant catering to military officials, but sometimes also civilians. It's just next to this building number 2 very close. Although it's really hidden by the trees. It's hard to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would this annex building also be known as the Dom JNA building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was previously called the Dom JNA, that is the hall of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you place a number 2 on the map as to approximately where that building was located?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: It looks the same. These are buildings of similar size. I really cannot be precise, I'm sorry. It could be a little to the left or a little to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But I think you said it was right next to the 1st Krajina Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Krzic, before you answer that next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, it appears that there was a mismark on the map. He was pointing to basically the same location as the 1st Krajina Corps headquarters when he was trying to indicate where number 2 was, and then I think somehow it got mismarked down by the river there. So I think if we could erase that mark. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you can look at photograph number 3. Could you identify for the Trial Chamber what that is a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: This is obviously the Bosna Hotel, and I'll try to place it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, if you could put a number 3 on the map.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krzic. What sorts of events took place at the hotel Bosna back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion the most important event was the arrival and the presence in that building of the chairman of the Security Council -- chairmen of the Security Council, Mr. Vance and Mr. Owen, and the following developments. There were many numerous -- there were numerous events and meetings of other nature, but from the viewpoint of the Democratic Action Party, it was the most important event.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Please take a look at photograph number 4 and tell us what this building was back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: This is the municipality building of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you put a number 4 where that building is located in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In relation to this building, where were the offices of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The SDS offices were opposite. There was a park in between with the monument to the fallen in the Second World War. Nowadays, there's an Orthodox church in its place, and the distance between two buildings was about 100 metres. This building housed the SDS offices, but very soon afterwards they were joined by the HDZ offices and the SDA offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krzic. And let me remind you, try to answer just my particular question. I know you are trying to provide as much information as possible for the Trial Chamber but since we have limited time. If you could take a look at photograph number 5, could you tell us what this building was back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I recognise the former SUP building, Secretariat of the Interior, later renamed CSB, which means Security Services Centre. The police, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And could you place a number 5 on the map approximately where that building was located.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Finally, we don't have a picture of this, but could you place a number 6 on the map where the Mali Logor prison was located in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, you said which number? 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Number 6, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this 65 ter exhibit 10213 be marked and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in your prior testimony you provided --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise to the counsel. The number will be P460.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, in your prior testimony, you provided evidence regarding the Serb plebiscite that was held in November 1991. Prior to that plebiscite, do you recall there being an SDS rally in Banja Luka on or about the 26th of October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you attend that rally?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was that rally covered by the media in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the media reported widely, but we also held a press conference on that rally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to watch a short news clip. This is 65 ter Exhibit 2303 for which there is also an English and B/C/S transcript. I believe it begins at 12 minutes and 36 seconds. If we could watch the whole video and then, Mr. Krzic, I'll have some questions after we've reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Anchor: ... while in Banja Luka the rally was freely held about joint leaving all Serbs in one state. There were plenty ethnic slurs. In the meantime, there are attempts at disputing the national rights of Muslims in Serbia by means of the Greater-Serbian oppression. Today's meeting in the centre of Banja Luka decorated by Yugoslav, Serbian and SDS insignia, explained the aims of the Serbian people's plebiscite set for 9 and 10 November, their wishes regarding the organisation of the country, the position of the Serbian people in it, and the aims and jurisdictions of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was founded two nights ago. The meeting was opened by Predrag Radic, Banja Luka Municipal Assembly President with the following message: "Twice they slaughtered us. We have forgiven but not forgotten. If they try to do the same for the third time, we shall neither forgive nor forget, regardless of how non-Christian it may be." Judging by the placards recorded on video by Ljubomir Paljevic and the reactions of the people present, Europe and its decisions have faired poorly in Banja Luka. Perhaps the strongest approval went to those who supported Slobodan Milosevic's refusal to sign The Hague documents. Limited time allows us to play only some of the audio clips. Speaker, Nikola Koljevic, BH Presidency member: We founded the Serbian Assembly in order to respond in a democratic, human, and civilised way - of which others proud themselves more than we do - that we will defend the rights of our people but we won't deprive others of their rights. Reporter: "Our legal system has been destroyed, we are economically exhausted thanks to Ante Markovic, but we will not give up the army," says Doctor Koljevic. Momcilo Krajisnik, BH Assembly President: "All the dark forces have for various reasons been harnessed to destroy our common fatherland, to tear us into pieces. And I hope we won't allow that." Reporter: Why will the Krajina TV be formed? Velibor Ostojic, Minister for Information in the BH Government: "We want to tell Europe the truth, to talk about justice, to say what's going on in these territories." Radovan Karadzic, SDS BH President: "The 9th and 10th November, by voting to remain in a joint, federal state with all the Serbian lands and all those who wish to stay with us, we hope to, once and for all, put a circle by state where there will be no traitors, a state that will not fall apart every 20 years or so." Reporter: We said that Europe fared poorly at today's meeting, most poorly perhaps in the part we cannot pass over in silence. One of those who spoke said that Vienna can be turned into Hiroshima. We shall put that down to careless formulation. We will finish our report by quoting Nikola Koljevic's words, "It's better for us to vote and vote down than shoot at each other."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, the video you just watched, what is that a video of?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: This is a rally, a mass meeting at which the then leaders of the Serb political block spoke in favour of the refusal of international political proposals with regard to the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There was preparation for -- for the Serb people to state their position to that effect, but here what we can see here apart from the different tone chosen by Dr. Koljevic, those are all flamboyant speeches which insighted uprising, destruction with clear indications of creating ethnically clean territories only for the Serb people. Maybe I should add that one of the participants went as far as to threaten -- to utter a threat which went beyond Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was aimed at neighbouring countries in Europe. And if I may refer to the newspaper "Glas" of Banja Luka which is controlled by Banja Luka, and we can see that it has a greater dimension because it's a call for the destruction of large European cities and not with the conventional weapons but nuclear weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: This is a statement that the Serbs are ready to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, again, let me remind you to try to keep your answers short, and I'll try to keep my questions more directed so that we can proceed in a very orderly fashion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, Your Honour, why is it relevant? It's 1991, out of scope with the indictment. The witness wasn't present at that meeting. His comment is out of the scope of the video-clip. Why is relevant for this trial? We are wasting time for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this video is relevant. It's all events leading up to April -- the beginning of April of 1992, and it gives -- it proceeded the plebiscite, so there's a number of issue that are important to our case and so we would submit that it is quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, whereas the question of context, I see what you are attempting to do. The reality is, this is a 92 ter witness, and Mr. Krgovic's observation about this being outside the scope of this evidence appears to have merit, so let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, this piece of evidence does go to the creation, the formation of the joint criminal enterprise, so it is a piece of evidence that we do want to admit. The purpose of this additional questioning of this witness is to bring in information that he is aware of. He did say that he was watching the media, it was well publicised. He appears to be familiar with what is being said at this rally, so I think this is a relevant topic for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We appreciate that everything has a context, Mr. Olmsted, but in order to make this trial manageable, let's keep it within the limits of what the -- within the scope of what this witness was tendered -- was called to testify to, having regard to the fact that he is a 92 ter witness. It seems to be we are wasting time wandering too far afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, in several places in your prior testimony you described Banja Luka during the April through December 1992 time-period as a concentration camp. You also described in various -- the various measures that were imposed by the Serb authorities on the non-Serb population that forced the non-Serb population to leave the Republika Srpska. I'm not going to ask you to repeat what you previously told the Tribunal, but I did want to ask some clarifying questions and show you some documents that are on our exhibit list. First of all, with regard to the dismissal of non-Serbs from their employment, I would like to show you 65 ter Exhibit 159. This document is headed the Krajina Autonomous Region Crisis Staff, or the ARK Crisis Staff. In 1992, Mr. Krzic, were you aware of the existence of an ARK Crisis Staff, at least in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who were the members of this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The president of the ARK by virtue of his position, and then the members were the chief of the CSB, he had to be a member, and there also had to be the representative of the army, and possibly not all the municipal parties but certainly for the Banja Luka municipality there was the mayor and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992, what kinds of decisions, just generally, was the ARK Crisis Staff issuing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Some decisions were accessible to us, and I suppose that they are mentioned in some documents, but the consequences of the decisions could be seen on the ground. We also have documentation about the laying off of non-Serbs which started with executive positions. The representatives of the staff even personally spoke about these decisions in the media, the printed media and the television. They mostly did so in person. Furthermore, the Crisis Staff called mobilisations. And the Crisis Staff also ordered some activities with regard to the property of non-Serbs. So the range of their decisions was from purely military issues to issues affecting the security of any non-Serb not only in Banja Luka but in the entire territory. I must say that there have been some decisions of a purely psychological nature. When I say that, I mean to make clear to the Judges that such a rally at which extermination is mentioned certainly isn't a folklore performance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, would you hear about these ARK Crisis Staff decisions through public statements or the media as well?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Most often through the statements made by some members of the ARK Crisis Staff, Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Radic, Mr. Kupresanin. It was difficult to get information directly because some information was published and other was not. But in practice, it was all implemented and acted upon without opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Taking a look at the 65 ter Exhibit 159, do you recall hearing about this decision about personnel of non-Serb ethnicity back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What was the effect of this decision on the non-Serb population, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Initially, we assumed that this would only apply to managers of companies. It was understood as a very serious warning. However, later on it became clear that the decision applied to all non-Serbs in positions where they could be replaced or where the others could do without them, so the first ones to be affected were medical staff and, you know, that medical staff is more important than any other. Well, to be brief I'll stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the second paragraph of the section one and it states that the decision applies to all socially owned enterprises. Mr. Krzic, in 1992 were companies in Banja Luka generally privately owned or state owned?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: 99 per cent were state owned or socially owned, and 1 or maybe 2 per cent may have been privately owned but they were mostly small shops such as florist shops, bakeries, candy shops and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we are at the point for the usual break.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, just to ease my mind and to be sure that I'm on the right list of documents for use with this witness, the video-clip you mentioned, 65 ter 2303, is it on your list of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is on our list. It's on our 65 ter list and also the list for this witness. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have to check something, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, just because you reminded me, perhaps we he could have that marked for identification just for future reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Marked for identification since that's your application.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P461 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, before the break you testified that 99 per cent of the companies in Banja Luka were socially owned back in 1992. Could you tell us if a Bosniak or a Croat working for a socially-owned company lost his or her job, what happened to his or her --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry, we may have a sound problem here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have problems hearing. I don't know why. Can you please say something now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Now it's all right. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll start again, Mr. Krzic. Prior to the break, you testified that approximately 99 per cent of the companies in Banja Luka in 1992 were socially owned. Could you tell us if a non-Serb working for a socially-owned company lost his or her job, what would happen to his or her right to accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: In most of the cases the enterprise they worked in would immediately raise the issue of accommodation. But I wouldn't say that this was done at a massive scale. Later on, though, when the security situation had worsened drastically, this was considered an important element in taking back the apartment from that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just so we are clear on this, later on when the security situation worsened, what would happen if a person lost their job in one of these companies? What would happen to their accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The argument was immediately raised that that person was no longer entitled to accommodation and that person would first be suggested to leave the apartment peacefully. So it would be suggested to them to apply to move out, and such agencies had already been established. If they failed to do that, there would be drastic threats, security threats, and they were sometimes realised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I suppose - or maybe I should ask the witness directly - I suppose this only goes for the flats that were owned by the companies and not for every flat; is that correct? I mean, I understand your testimony to be that if a person was fired from the socially-owned company in which he worked or she worked, then the flat that went with the job also was lost, but it could be that some of the workers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in their own flats and my question was then if they would also lose the right to live in such non-company-owned flats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, taking a look at this decision that's currently on the screen, to what extent was this ARK Crisis Staff decision implemented against non-Serbs in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question correctly. Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. We have this decision here that states that only personnel of Serbian ethnicity may hold certain positions, and my question to you is to what extent this decision was, in fact, implemented in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: That measure was implemented gradually or successively. If I may, I'll mention a very telling example. It was mostly implemented successfully through a longer period of time. When somebody was replaced from a position, or not merely from a position, but possibly was laid off as a couple of hundred doctors were laid off in five or six months, the apartments were not taken away from them immediately, but once the situation had worsened and a Serb population was withdrawing from Croatia or other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the measure of taking away the apartment would follow. If a doctor, the head of a hospital in Banja Luka was replaced and he would be placed in a position of head of an infirmary, he would have had to leave his older, big apartment and move into a smaller one that went with his new position. And over 400 people, I believe, doctors and medical staff, were laid off, and once they lost their jobs for good, they would have to leave their apartments and Banja Luka, and I can mention the names of the heads of the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, I want to refocus you on my question. The decision in front of you simply relates to personnel of non-Serb ethnicity being removed from their post. And perhaps you could tell us, if you could provide us with an estimate, by the end of 1992 approximately what percentage of the non-Serbs in Banja Luka municipality had lost their jobs as a result of this kind of decision?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I don't have any accurate estimates. The closest most accurate estimates I have are those about doctors and professionals in hospitals and public health. You know that medical staff is the most important service for human life and a -- and at least 50 per cent of non-Serb doctors and medical staff were laid off. And the percentage that applies to schools was roughly the same, and it would reach 100 per cent very soon in the following year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: How would you learn about these various dismissals of non-Serbs from their posts in companies or in the government?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: It was sometimes made public because not only executive personnel but all work-places where non-Serbs worked were soon affected. I don't know whether there was a special decision of the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region, but in practice it was called technological surplus which was possible because the country was at war. But the measure that ensued was mass layoffs of non-Serbs, and you could read in the papers about it in "Glas." And then these dismissals started at schools, teachers were laid off under various pretext, whoever refused to write in Cyrillic script was fired within 24 hours, and nobody ever complained, it's clear why. And I believe it was also the Crisis Staff that decided that all those must be laid off who don't respond the call for mobilisation. And that decision and practice was applied also to the entire family of that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd like to admit 65 ter Exhibit 159 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a few "Glas" newspaper articles from between April and July 1992. And you've had a chance to look at these and review them prior to testifying here today. So we'll go through them -- we'll view them quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: The first one is 65 ter Exhibit 2800.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krzic, since you've reviewed these recently, I don't expect you to have to read through them all again, but just take a quick look to verify that you did in fact see them earlier.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let's now take a look at 65 ter Exhibit 2801.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, if you could just verify that you took a look at this article before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, if we could have on the screen 65 ter Exhibit 2803.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, during the April to December 1992 time-period, could you tell us how objective did you consider the "Glas" newspaper to be as far as fairly reporting the views of all ethnicities in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Of course, at that time you could not look for objectivity in the way you would in a democratic society, but we were happy when what we were saying was reflected even approximately, and we continued to be quite satisfied until about the middle, that is the end of 1991, and beginning of 1992, and I'm talking especially about "Glas" which is a regional newspaper, a daily. And, of course, we could place our interviews there, if necessary, in every issue, and this regular reporting, I would say, continued until they started dismissing both Croats and Serbs from the newspaper. I think they even dismissed Serbs who were in mixed marriages so that after that time we stopped giving them interviews because each time we tried, we would end up reading a completely different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to be clear, towards whom did you believe the "Glas" newspaper to be biased after the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I believe the witness added a last sentence at the very end of 32, 18, and if it can be recorded because the transcript doesn't show that sentence which he said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Krzic, did you hear my question? I'll repeat it. In your view, towards whom was the "Glas" newspaper biased after the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Already towards the end of 1991 some bias could be felt, especially towards the Croat population for understandable reasons. And then generally it spread to all non-Serbs, including the Romas and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to be clear, was the "Glas" newspaper biased towards non-Serbs, or was it biased against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Against, against. I believe I'm speaking quite clearly. I don't understand why you were misled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Krzic, I just wanted to make sure it was clear for the record. Did this bias appear only to the "Glas" newspaper, or would it apply to other forms of media in Banja Luka during this 1992 time-period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: It applied to all the media. For instance, in Radio Banja Luka all non-Serbs were laid off, and they were not only laid off, but before they were laid off, they were ordered to apply in a compulsory fashion a new type of organisation and editing both in the press and on the radio, and thus all the folk songs which were common to all of us had to be destroyed on videotape and in records, to be burnt in our yards. Nobody dared risk put on a folk song with a Bosniak or a Croat background.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Returning to the three articles I just showed you, and in particular the one in front of you right now, were these the kinds of articles that were appearing in the "Glas" newspaper concerning the dismissals of non-Serbs from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Except there's one idiosyncrasy you forgot to mention. When I speak of non-Serb population, I include mixed marriages. For instance, in this particular article, the board of managers is an Assembly of dervishes. We see a reference to one of their leading experts, Slobodan Cvijetic, an electrical engineer, who was leading a company producing very sophisticated electronic products, but his particular weakness is that he had a Croat wife, and this Cvijetic did not immediately proceed with dismissing Croats from his institute, from his company, and this is a typical example of, how shall I call it, racist action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Since you brought up this topic of Mr. Cvijetic, generally what happened to Serb managers of companies who refused to implement dismissal decisions against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: They could not remain in their positions. It was clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the third paragraph of this article in front of you, Exhibit 2803, Mr. Brdjanin is quoted as saying that: "Muslim and Croat executives have been replaced in almost 95 per cent of companies ..." Was that an accurate statement by Brdjanin at this time when this article was written?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: It probably was. I can see the names here of the people who were replaced, people with an international reputation as scientists and researchers, and I thought it was the end of 1992 here, but we see that he is giving this statement in July. It's possible that he did not include by that time lower-level executives, such as heads of workshops, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would ask that 65 ter Exhibits 2800, 2801 and 2803 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We strongly object, Your Honours. I believe my learned friend thinks about -- is referring to the previous three articles which he showed to the witness, the "Glas" articles. Are these the documents that you are offering for evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We are -- the one that's currently on the screen which is 2803 as well as our two that the witness had previously looked at that are essentially dealing with the same issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, you know that the Stanisic Defence has many times already explained why we feel that all these articles from that period are -- cannot be relied upon. This witness, in fact, confirms that, he says they were biased articles. These three articles are nothing else but the press conferences or the interviews of Radoslav Brdjanin. The Prosecution, thanks to the rules of this Tribunal, has the opportunity to offer adjudicated fact from the Brdjanin trial. These documents are relevant for Brdjanin trial, and they have been presented there as evidence. The Trial Chamber came up to a certain conclusion concerning these particular documents. I don't really see any need for us to get -- to admit these documents. First of all, they are not reliable, they are not relevant for the accused, and the third, the witness himself confirms that the "Glas" in 1992 was highly biased against non-Serbs. Therefore, the connection between this witness and these documents is non-existent. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, since you are on your feet, could you remind me, I recall that this issue of the newspaper articles has arisen before, and my recollection is that the previous practice of the Tribunal, the jurisprudence, does not hold them inadmissible per se, but my reservation is that the -- when we would have visited this before, the question the nexus with the particular witness, could you remind me as to how we may have dealt with it previously in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, as far as I know in majority of the cases, these articles when offered were admitted. We did -- we did raise our objection, and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal stands on the point, as far as I know, that it goes to the weight of the particular document or evidence. But just the same, I believe it is my duty to raise the attention of the Trial Chamber to this because, Your Honours, you have to keep in mind that all these articles which are offered are written within the relevant period of time in 1992, there's a war going on, and there's a special warfare which is done through media, which is, I believe, very clear from these articles from all sides. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it strikes us that whereas as I indicated to Mr. Zecevic, we are quite aware that the jurisprudence is that newspaper articles are not, per se, inadmissible, that in this particular case, we don't see how they assist the Chamber or add to what the witness has testified to in terms of his own knowledge of these matters, and we don't see that on balance that the articles themselves have much of any probative value. So that is why we are reluctant to accede to the application that they be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, certainly you'll be able to take whatever -- decide whatever weight you want to give these articles based upon the testimony of the various witnesses. However, these articles certainly corroborate this witness's testimony. They are written, as Defence counsel mentioned, during the relevant time-period, they cover a very relevant issue relating to persecution in Banja Luka which we do charge in the indictment, and just for us to assume that you are going to completely accept this witness's testimony without potential corroborating testimony or evidence such as exhibits, articles, and newspapers, which albeit may be biased towards the Serbs certainly provide information as it to what information is going out to the community during this time period, and certainly this witness has testified that some of the information that Brdjanin was providing was most likely accurate, for instance the extent of the dismissals. And also let me just mention that Brdjanin is a member of the joint criminal enterprise in this matter, a member of the ARK Crisis Staff, so it is quite relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see your point, but I would alert you to this, Mr. Olmsted, that even if they were -- even if we were to admit them, it is something that the Chamber would have to consider very very carefully, because as Mr. Zecevic succinctly pointed out, the newspaper articles themselves were an instrument of warfare in this exercise, so at the end of the day, the point of admitting them is something which isn't immediately apparent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber rules by majority that the documents would be admitted. So they may, accordingly, be marked as exhibits. Judge Delvoie dissenting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P463, P464, and P465.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little bit reluctant to show the next exhibit, but talk about taking the steam out of my drive here. 65 ter Exhibit 2802. If we could have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krzic, this is another article that you had a chance to look at prior to testifying here today. And it's not from the "Glas" newspaper. It's dated 18 June 1992, and it discusses the dismissal of non-Serb employees from the hospital in Banja Luka. And I believe earlier in your testimony you were talking about extensive dismissals of non-Serbs from the hospitals, and I ask you, does this generally -- is this generally consistent with your recollection as to what was happening during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What effect did these health care dismissals have on the rest of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The rest of the population non-Serbs were practically left without health care. There were no private physicians at the time. Why did they believe they were deprived of health care? Because they did not dare to go and see an exclusively Serbian medical staff. They did not dare because by that time there had been many cases when they were simply refused admittance. There were some serious patients with kidney conditions who simply disappeared. The treatment of such patients was horrible. Perhaps the best proof are non-Serbs with cancer who did not dare go to the medical centre. One doctor, Vesna Krmatic [phoen] a Croat, distributed to them some sort of powder because she could not give them real medicine for their condition. That was the catastrophe that reigned at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all the caveats that were expressed by the Trial Chamber and everyone else, may this 65 ter Exhibit 2802 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't need to explain again why I object, thank you very much, Your Honours, but I do object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move on to another topic --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit P466, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm off my rhythm right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your prior testimony, you described how between April and December 1992 there were explosions practically every night in Banja Luka resulting in the destruction of non-Serb businesses and homes. Can you tell us based on what you could see and what you knew and heard, what were the police doing to prevent the destruction of non-Serb property?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I know that non-Serbs in some very rare cases tried to get the protection of the police, but I'm not aware that any perpetrators were ever arrested except perhaps in some exceptions. If a Croat or Bosniak, for instance, knew somebody on the police force and bribed them, I'm not aware of such cases, but I know that down-town let alone in the suburbs, in all cases involving explosions, the perpetrators were neither prevented from this action or arrested afterwards. In the middle of the market, soldiers would come, supposedly drunk, to beat up the owner of a flower shop, and if he did not sign over his shop to them, he would be targeted by a bombing the same night. I know specific names for all these cases. The police, to the best of my knowledge, never did anything to prevent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your prior testimony, you mentioned that the Serb authorities imposed a curfew in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter Exhibit 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this document has in its heading the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina Republic Secretariat for National Defence, and it's dated 4 May 1992. Mr. Krzic, what was in your mind, what was the ARK Secretariat of National Defence around this time-period in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: You can see from this order that they passed, among other things, security-related decisions for the entire municipality and beyond. That is, they had unlimited rights of issuing orders and probably also of holding people responsible. It was their task to order mobilisation and everything that follows from that. So they were a body, I don't know what to call it, but obviously in charge of the overall security situation among others in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In May 1992, what was the ethnicity of the members of the secretariat, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were exclusively of Serb ethnicity. Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Brdjanin, Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Radic, General Talic, before him it was Uzelac. For awhile there was also the Prime Minister Kasagic. I don't know whether he stayed on later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at number 4 of this decision, and according to this document it imposes a curfew between 2200 hours and 0500 hours. Who enforced this curfew in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Obviously the police. Well, I don't want to say any more, the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And from what you could see, was this curfew equally enforced against all the ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Most certainly not. For non-Serbs a violation of the curfew meant not only -- or constituted not only an offence to be sanctioned administratively, it was also a deadly threat because a non-Serb found on the street during the curfew would not only immediately be beaten up and robbed, but he also risked losing their life because such things happened also in plain daylight, not only during the curfew. But this was also a warning for the entire population, including Serbs, I mean civilians, not to move about town. I had -- personally had the chance to convince myself that the town was completely empty. This place, Copenhagen, is also a quiet town, but there and then, you could hardly see anybody because the times were unsafe and they could -- whoever moved about could easily become evicted. But it was also well known that this curfew was a sort of indirect protection for those who went about robbing at the time, entering houses, threatening with weapons, et cetera, so this was a kind of protection for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that leads to my next question, which is this curfew, what effect did it have on non-Serb businesses?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I have just told you that this was a total restriction, but explosive devices against private property mostly went off during the night. Cultural facilities of non-Serbs were also mostly attacked at night. There are witnesses to confirm that it was the police who first set fire to the mosques and when that didn't work out, they would return. All that went on during the curfew. There are witnesses to confirm that. As for the property of non-Serbs in town, that was a town -- a time when they couldn't expect their property to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Under number 5 of this decision, it requires the surrender of illegal weapons by 11 May 1992. Who enforced this decision?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And against whom was this particular decision enforced against?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Against non-Serbs, of course, for the simple reason that if it had been enforced against the Serbs, you would have had to deploy massive forces of the police to take away the weapons that were distributed at a massive scale to Serbs. In the centre of town, there were deliveries of huge quantities of weapons that were distributed to Serb families, so this obviously didn't refer to these weapons, but such weapons for which there were permits such as hunting weapons, et cetera, but those who did have other weapons didn't bring the weapons to the police, but mostly discarded them by the river or so because going to the police and openly state that you belong to another ethnicity and have weapons, well, you can imagine what that meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned the distribution of weapons around Banja Luka on a massive scale. Were you able to observe this happening, and if so, who was distributing these weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I personally saw that in the local community of Hiseta there was a restaurant called Baraka, and I was invited by some people I knew to witness the distribution of weapons. There were trucks there and with boxes on it full of weapons and ammunition. And in the evening it was distributed. And I received other information, similar information of such weapons distribution also in the neighbourhood where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were the person --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I believe the witness explained which trucks, whom the trucks belonged to, so if you can please clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could be a little more specific as to the actual persons who were distributing these weapons that you observed. Were they wearing any uniforms, did you recognise any of the individuals as being a member of any kind of organisation whether it be the military or the police or another organisation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: On this concrete case they were wearing plain uniforms, so they were regular soldiers, not special units. Olive green uniforms. And I looked at that from a distance, but I can't say that I saw the police on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness said I couldn't. I can't say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what about weapons that were lawfully owned by non-Serbs, were they allowed to keep their lawfully-owned weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: No. They were ordered to return their weapons, and I was rather -- when they came to my house on one occasion, they took the weapon I had without any questions. It was a small calibre pistol that I really needed to defend myself because there had been shots fired at my door.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would move for 65 ter Exhibit 107 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P467, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your prior testimony, you state that Serb authorities established a number of check-points throughout the Banja Luka town and municipality, and that non-Serbs were maltreated at these check-points. Can you tell us who was manning these check-points?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: We can say that it was exclusively the police, although in the early days in some parts of town there were attempts to organise, well maybe not check-points, but joint patrols, that was in 1991, but that soon came to an end. Then the police took over exclusively and they wore police uniforms. Did you ask anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I will now. How were the police maltreating non-Serbs at these check-points? If you can describe that briefly.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: They were asking for personal documents and if you showed them -- showed your documents, they sometimes wouldn't return them to you. You could be hit and it often happened, and if somebody tried to come from the suburbs, if they were non-Serb and tried to bring agricultural produce into town, they were either ordered to return or taken away or in some cases they would have to discard them on the spot. And the farmers later tried to bring that into town through Serbs who were their friends, so in such a way wood was brought into town, which was important to live through the winter, and I also bought firewood from -- in this manner. So obviously one of the objectives was to prevent non-Serbs to move through town and keep them inside their enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move to another topic now. In your prior testimony you mentioned that non-Serbs were evicted from their businesses and their homes, and these businesses and homes were then given to Serb soldiers who were returning from the front lines. Can you tell us who issued these eviction orders in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: There are some concrete cases that I know, but let me first tell you, often times there weren't any orders at all. Simply if a Serb, especially if they had come to Banja Luka with their family and wanted to enter an apartment, they had force at their disposal and could do so by force. And I can mention an example from my own family. My father and brother were evicted from their apartment and came to me, and they were evicted without any -- without any statement of reason. Even the president of Merhamet was evicted and another who didn't want to leave his apartment, well, to him they placed a bomb there so that he fell through the floor to the apartment below.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Before we get off too much off track, where you say that there were cases where orders were actually issued, who would issue those orders? Would there be an entity that would issue an order evicting a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the municipality Crisis Staff or staffs and the removal agency, but I can't say what their share was in all that and what the share of sheer force was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In 1992 were you aware of a policy concerning property exchanges between non-Serbs living in Banja Luka and Serbs moving into the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that very well from my own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Please take a look at 65 ter Exhibit 143. And we can see from the heading that this is an ARK Crisis Staff conclusion dated 28 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page in both the English and B/C/S and look at conclusion number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, conclusion number 7 states that: "If Muslims and Croats, or members of the SDA or HDZ wish to leave or move out of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, they must enable the endangered Serbian people, against whom unprecedented genocide is being conducted, to move collectively into their places, i.e., they must facilitate an exchange based on reciprocity." Mr. Krzic, was this generally the exchange policy that you were aware of that was in existence in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: That was general knowledge, but I repeat, from the experience of my immediate and -- immediate relatives and remote relatives and from my own experience, I can tell you who was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were these exchanges voluntary?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: By no means.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you please describe to us how these exchanges actually took place in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: There were several variants. There was also private initiative where people would exchange property without accompanying documentation, I can mention examples for that too. And when they went to Croatia or other places in Bosnia, they wouldn't find anything at all or, say, a barn instead of a house. So the removal agency was first run privately by Ms. Perka and her husband. They came to the apartment of my parents in 1991 and offered an exchange for a house on the island of Krk. I immediately understood that if I were to do that, that act of mine would effect the other population very negatively so I refused. The agency conducted a large number of both successful and unsuccessful exchanges. Some were fair and many others were unfair. When we started sending such information abroad, then at some point in late 1992, I believe, it was transformed into an official removal agency which speaking of Banja Luka, was linked to the municipality, and they had their own price list for these services with the exchange of property or without. First -- at first you needed a huge amount of documentation, and people would sign that because they were forced to do so, and later on it was all -- it all became very simple because as Mr. Brdjanin said, it is important that they leave even if we give them passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just a clarification in your testimony just now you said that they came to your apartment of your parents to offer an exchange in 1991. Was that in fact the correct year?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was in late 1991. I can find the exact date. But certainly before April 1992. Before the 4th of April 1992. So the efforts were being put into this willing exchange and departure as early as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the SDA or for that matter since you probably worked with them to certain respect, the HDZ, did they take a particular position with regard to these exchange -- these exchanges? Were they opposed to it, or were they in favour of it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I must say that both the SDA and the HDZ clearly condemned such activities and said so clearly at several press conferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would move for the admission of this Exhibit 65 ter 143 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P468, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, for those non-Serbs who did not exchange their properties, what happened to their property if they left Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Speaking about real estate, there was no chance for them to leave it to somebody to look after their property. That property was immediately taken into possession by somebody else. Mostly people who returned from the front line or refugee Serbs from Croatia. During later periods such as 1993, the municipality put up their personnel there. They would send a commission for such property and that it's in my case and they evicted my parents in the process, and they developed a formal institutional approach to that. They would establish that willingly abandoned property can be used for the needs of the municipal institutions. And that was the way of taking over such property, including all furniture unless it had been taken away or stolen before that. So if somebody would go to Zagreb provisionally, that was the most frequent place where people would go. I went there for treatment, medical treatment, and even though I had a permission to go there, such people who left even for a short time couldn't go back to their property because it had already been occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter Exhibit 10216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you are a few seconds short of the next break. Would this be a convenient point to interrupt your --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, while the witness is being escorted back to the stand, I would alert you that over the two hours you've requested, you've exhausted 1 hour 24 minutes. Sorry, 1 hour, 34 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm certainly making progress here. This is a unique witness in that we do not have non-Serb witnesses from Banja Luka talking about what was going on in Banja Luka. I'd ask the Trial Chamber's a little bit of indulgence in case I go over that. I know that Defence counsel, we can ask them, I'm not sure whether they oppose if we do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The guillotine will come down at two hours, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Otherwise, you could have chosen to lead this witness as viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'd like to jump ahead then and if we could have 65 ter Exhibit 10214 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, this is a "Glas" article dated 16 April 1992. Mr. Krzic, do you recall reading this article in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This article describes a 15 April meeting that you attended in Banja Luka with Mayor Predrag Radic and SJB chief Vladimir Tutus in April 1992. Do you recall attending that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This article, if we scroll down a little bit, at least on the English, reports that the reason for this meeting was a public statement made by Stojan Zupljanin. Could you tell us what precisely was the statement by Zupljanin that prompted this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Chief responsible for the general security of the citizens of Banja Luka. Mr. Zupljanin had all our attention whenever he spoke to the press because he was not a politician, he was an officer of an institution that was supposed to hold primary responsibility for us at the time. And when he stated that he could not guarantee complete security, and mind you, security in this case means physical security and the safety of our property, we found it shattering, and we could see for ourselves that our security was in great jeopardy even then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At this meeting with the government representatives and the police representatives, what concerns did you raise to them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we stated the things that were common knowledge by that time. If I recall well, the first thing mentioned were murders that were happening already without anyone being identified. Then we discussed the security of property, the daily looting and nightly explosions and bombings and of course one of the main things was that general panic had overtaken the town. Everyone was wondering what was going to happen and many people could still vividly remember the horrors of the Second World War. It was fear that drove us to speak to Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to be clear for the record, the crimes that you described as well as the statement made by Zupljanin, against whom were these crimes being perpetrated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part against non-Serbs. It's true that there were also crimes against Serbs, but they were mainly accounted for by settlements of personal accounts or settlements of accounts between two or more mafia gangs who were sort of dividing up the territory and wanted to have as big a chunk of the looting for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What response to all this information about the crimes and the treatment of non-Serbs that you were conveying at this meeting did you receive from the police and government representatives at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: We were very disappointed by his response, the response of Mr. Radic primarily, who said that the situation was even worse for Serbs outside of the Bosnian Krajina. He mentioned, and it is stated here, the territory under the control of the HVO such as Tomislavgrad, et cetera. We were astounded, and we saw a kind of continuity in that whatever was going on in Banja Luka was seen as reciprocity against what was happening to Serbs outside. For instance, Dr. Koljevic said to the press and to the television, What are you up in arms for when 10.000 Serbs were dismissed in Croatia. We made later some attempts through the headquarters of the Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. This kind of response that Radic gave to your concerns, was this unusual, or was this the typical response you would be receiving from authorities, the Serb authorities in Banja Luka when you raised these issues?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: It was the typical response for that time. Later on as the situation escalated, it was out of the question to even complain. For this also you have documents. Anyone who complained, risked their life. There is enough evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what was SJB chief Tutus's response to the issues you were raising at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: This, what's his name. Excuse me, I can't remember the last name. I know it begins with a T. Yes, yes, we have his name on the record. He tried to mention our representative on the police force, Mr. Bajazit Jahic but by that time Bajazit Jahic had already been dismissed as a Bosniak because he had refused to sign the document on loyalty. And this document on loyalty also implied availability for the front line, the front line service. His name was Tutus, is that who you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's right. Now, in your prior testimony, you mentioned attending a meeting with Cyrus Vance and Lord Owen in Banja Luka in September of 1992 and at that meeting you raised once again a number of concerns regarding treatment of the non-Serb population in Banja Luka and elsewhere. When you met with Vance and Owen on that occasion, can you tell us the names of the Bosnian Serb officials who were present?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM KRZIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you who was present at the talks directly with Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance because various groups came to these talks. We came as a group from the SDA. There was a group from the SDS and from the HDZ, but I can't tell you who was sitting in the hall. It was a hall double the size of this one, and this led to a conference room where the co-chairmen were sitting. In that hall, at that hour you could see the highest representatives of various community, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Kupresanin, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Zupljanin, Mr. Brdjanin, I believe Vukic was there as well.
